citation: PRIMARY: SmartBear Software, 'Best Practices for Peer Code Review' white paper (Cisco study, wrapped up 2006; also chapter 5 of 'Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review', Jason Cohen), opened via a mirrored PDF at https://files-cdn.cnblogs.com/files/dangjian/BestPracticesForPeerCodeReview.pdf and the live SmartBear page https://smartbear.com/learn/code-review/best-practices-for-peer-code-review/. SECONDARY 1: Sadowski, Soederberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli, 'Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google', ICSE-SEIP 2018, https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/4476.pdf. SECONDARY 2: Bosu, Greiler, Bird, 'Characteristics of Useful Code Reviews: An Empirical Study at Microsoft', MSR 2015, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/bosu2015useful.pdf. NOT OPENED: Baum, Schneider, Bacchelli 2019; di Biase et al. change decomposition experiment (PeerJ CS 2019); Rigby and Bird 2013.
source_tier: SmartBear/Cisco: vendor research (white paper, not peer reviewed). Google ICSE-SEIP 2018 and Microsoft MSR 2015: peer-reviewed conference papers from industry labs.
access_status: SmartBear white paper: fully read via mirrored PDF (date of the mirror copy unverified; the live SmartBear page was read only via a fetch summary). Google paper: fully downloaded and text-searched. Microsoft paper: downloaded and read for the change-size section and Fig. 8; not read end to end. Baum 2019, di Biase 2019 (HTTP 403), Rigby and Bird 2013: not opened, search snippets only. SmartBear original 2006 chapter 5 of Best Kept Secrets: not opened [uncertain].
sponsor_and_incentive: SmartBear sells Code Collaborator, the review tool used to collect the Cisco data and to run the study. The study was conducted by SmartBear with Cisco's MeetingPlace team, so the vendor has a commercial interest in code review findings. Google and Microsoft studies: authors are employees (plus academic co-authors) studying their own companies; no product being sold.
exact_quotes: SmartBear white paper, section 1: "Review fewer than 200-400 lines of code at a time. The Cisco code review study (see sidebar for details) showed that for optimal effectiveness, developers should review fewer than 200-400 lines of code (LOC) at a time. Beyond that, the ability to find defects diminishes. At this rate, with the review spread over no more than 60-90 minutes, you should get a 70-90% yield; in other words, if 10 defects existed, you'd find 7-9 of them."

SmartBear white paper, section 1: "Defect density is the number of defects per 1000 lines of code. As the number of lines of code under review grows beyond 300, defect density drops off considerably."
SmartBear white paper, Figure 1 caption: "Defect density dramatically decreases when the number of lines of inspection goes above 200, and is almost zero after 400."

SmartBear white paper, section 2: "Aim for an inspection rate of less than 300-500 LOC/hour ... reviewing faster than 400-500 LOC/hour results in a severe drop-off in effectiveness. And at rates above 1000 LOC/hour, you can probably conclude that the reviewer isn't actually looking at the code at all."

SmartBear white paper, sidebar: "encompassing 2500 code reviews, 50 programmers, and 3.2 million lines of code at Cisco Systems. For ten months, the study tracked the MeetingPlace product team, distributed across Bangalore, Budapest, and San Jose." Rules: all code reviewed before check-in to Perforce; Code Collaborator used; in-person meetings not allowed.

SmartBear white paper, section 4 (about author preparation, not size): "We took a random sample of 300 reviews to investigate, and the evidence definitively showed that the reviewers were indeed carefully reviewing the code - there were just fewer bugs."

SmartBear live page (fetch summary of headings): "Review fewer than 400 lines of code at a time"; "developers should review no more than 200 to 400 lines of code (LOC) at a time."; "SmartBear research shows a significant drop in defect density at rates faster than 500 LOC per hour." The page does not mention pull requests.

Google ICSE-SEIP 2018, Review size: "At Google, over 35% of the changes under consideration modify only a single file and about 90% modify fewer than 10 files. Over 10% of changes modify only a single line of code, and the median number of lines modified is 24."

Google 2018, review speed: "developers have to wait for initial feedback on their change a median time of under an hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large changes. The overall (all code sizes) median latency for the entire review process is under 4 hours."

Google 2018, discussion: "Previous studies have found that the number of useful comments decreases [11, 14] and the review latency increases [8, 24] as the size of the change increases." And: "A correlation between change size and review quality is acknowledged by Google and developers are strongly encouraged to make small, incremental changes."

Google 2018: "the average number of comments per change grows with the number of lines changed, reaching a peak of 12.5 comments per change for changes of about 1250 lines. Changes larger than this often contain auto-generated code or large deletions, resulting in a lower average number of comments."

Microsoft MSR 2015, Sec. on changeset size: "The trendline shows that as number of files in the change increases, the proportion of comments that are useful drops. This result supports Rigby's recommendation for smaller changesets." And: "Our results suggest that review effectiveness decreases with the number of files in the change set. Therefore, we recommend that developers submit smaller and incremental changes whenever possible."
key_claims: (1) SmartBear/Cisco: in lightweight tool-based reviews at Cisco, defect density (defects found per 1000 LOC) fell as the lines under review per review rose, falling off beyond ~300 LOC and near zero after ~400; hence the advice to review 200-400 LOC at a time over 60-90 minutes. Separately, faster inspection rates (above 400-500 LOC/hour) coincided with fewer defects found. (2) Google 2018: most changes are small (median 24 lines, ~90% under 10 files); first-feedback latency is under an hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large ones; the paper cites earlier work for the claim that useful comments fall and latency rises with size. The Google paper does not itself measure defect detection against size. (3) Microsoft 2015 (Bosu, Greiler, Bird): the proportion of useful review comments drops as the number of files in a change grows (Fig. 8, x-axis 0 to 40 files); authors recommend smaller, incremental changesets.
headline_figures: SmartBear: '200-400 lines of code at a time' (white paper); live page heading says 'fewer than 400 lines'. Unit: LOC per review. Comparison: defect density across reviews of different sizes. Date: study ended 2006. MATCHES the lead's '400 lines' only loosely: the paper says 200-400 and shows the drop starting near 200-300; it does not say 'sharply above 400', it says defect density is 'almost zero after 400'.

SmartBear: defect density drops 'beyond 300' LOC and 'dramatically' above 200 (Figure 1 caption). Defect density = defects per 1000 LOC. Note this metric is partly an artefact: a larger review gives the reviewer less time per line, and the paper itself frames low density as lower reviewer effectiveness, though the white paper also says low density can mean fewer bugs existed (author preparation finding).

SmartBear: inspection rate under 300-500 LOC/hour (section heading) and severe drop-off above 400-500 LOC/hour; 1000+ LOC/hour implies not looking. Unit: LOC reviewed per hour. This is a speed figure, not a change-size figure.
SmartBear: 60-90 minute review window and '70-90% yield' (7-9 of 10 existing defects). The yield figure's basis is not explained in the white paper [uncertain].
Sample: 2500 reviews, 50 programmers, 3.2 million LOC, ten months, MeetingPlace team across Bangalore, Budapest and San Jose.

'10 files' in the lead: NOT in SmartBear. The only 10-file figure found is Google's descriptive statistic that about 90% of Google changes modify fewer than 10 files. That is a size distribution, not a quality threshold. Microsoft's figure 8 plots usefulness density against 0-40 files with a declining trendline but no cliff at 10 files in the text I read [uncertain on exact curve values].

Google: median change 24 lines; over 35% single-file; ~90% under 10 files; initial feedback median under 1 hour (small) vs about 5 hours (very large); overall median review latency under 4 hours; mean reviewing time 3.2 hours per week (median 2.6). Data: review logs of 9 million changes, 12 interviews, survey of 44 (from the Google abstract page).

Microsoft: ~1.5 million review comments from five projects classified by a trained classifier; 844 comments manually classified for training; a figure of 34.50% non-useful comments is cited by later work.
sample_and_method: SmartBear/Cisco: observational data automatically collected by Code Collaborator from 2500 reviews (50 developers, 3.2M LOC, 10 months, one product team). The white paper says defect data was checked on a random sample of 300 reviews (in the author-preparation discussion). Defects are those logged in the tool by reviewers, so 'defect density' is a count of logged findings per 1000 LOC, not seeded or independently verified bugs. The reviews were of code changes before check-in to Perforce, i.e. changelist reviews, not pull requests (Perforce, 2005-06, no mention of pull requests). Google: mixed methods (interviews, survey, logs of 9 million changes); size analysis is descriptive. Microsoft: interviews plus classifier-labelled comments; usefulness is defined by whether a comment triggers a nearby code change, so 'usefulness density' is not defect detection.
limitations: Stated or visible: SmartBear data is vendor-collected, single team, single company, 2005-06, and has no published methodology, confidence intervals or peer review that I could find. Defect density falls with size partly by construction (fixed attention spread over more lines, fewer logged defects per line), and the paper cannot separate 'reviewer missed defects' from 'fewer defects existed'. Review size is confounded with author, code type and preparation (the paper itself shows author preparation sharply cuts defects found). I found no independent replication of the 200-400 LOC figure [uncertain: not exhaustively searched]. The 400 figure is a recommendation derived from a chart, not a stated threshold in the data. It is not a pull-request study. Google's paper is descriptive on size and borrows its quality claim from other studies. Microsoft's metric is comment usefulness, not escaped defects, and all five projects are from one company. I could not open the Baum et al. 2019 controlled experiment or the di Biase et al. decomposition experiment; a search summary suggests the latter found no effect of decomposition on defects found, but that is unverified and the text was garbled [uncertain].
what_a_leader_can_do: Supported: set an expectation of small, incremental changes; both Google (strongly encouraged, median 24 lines) and Microsoft (recommend smaller changesets) support this, and Google ties small size to faster first feedback (under 1 hour vs about 5 hours). Evidence strength: moderate for speed and comment usefulness, weak and vendor-sourced for defect detection thresholds. Supported, weakly: give reviewers enough time per line (SmartBear's inspection-rate result). Not supported: citing a hard '400 lines or 10 files' cliff. For an AI-agent context, none of these sources studied agent-generated changes, so they say nothing direct about review of agent output volume; they support the general point that review quality depends on how much is put in front of the reviewer and how long they have.
overlap_with_site_essays: Strongest overlap with Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part (reviewer attention and time per line) and Checking Isn't Catching (more checking effort does not equal more defects caught; SmartBear's inspection-rate finding is a data point). Light overlap with The Verification Gap and What It Takes to Trust Agent Output (large volume of unreviewed change). I have not re-read the essays this run; overlap judged from titles and the task brief [uncertain].
